analysis.one_liner: Opens more federal offshore waters to oil and gas drilling, backs coal-to-liquids plants with federal loans, and extends renewable energy tax credits.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2008, the bill was referred to five House committees and never received a vote or committee action before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was an "all of the above" energy package written during the 2008 gasoline price spike. It would have opened most federal offshore waters outside the Gulf of Mexico to oil and gas leasing, repealed oil shale restrictions, and given up to six coal-to-liquids plants federal loans in which the government pays the companies whenever oil prices fall below a set floor. It also extended and expanded tax credits for wind, solar, geothermal, and other renewables, created a $40 billion clean-energy research fund paid for with drilling royalties, and directed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to shine light on energy market speculation. It was referred to five House committees, none of which ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Energy industries gain the most: oil and gas companies get new offshore lease opportunities on the Outer Continental Shelf and renewed oil shale access; coal companies get federal standby loans with price floors plus a larger advanced-coal investment credit; the nuclear industry gets reauthorized federal programs and an export-promotion working group; renewable energy developers and manufacturers get extended and expanded tax credits. Households get smaller, indirect benefits — residential solar, wind, and geothermal heat pump credits, a plug-in vehicle credit, a bicycle-commuting tax break, and more public data on energy market speculation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, nuclear, and renewable energy companies

how_it_helps.text: Extends and expands renewable electricity tax credits: wind through 2009, biomass, geothermal, hydropower, landfill gas, and trash combustion through 2011, and adds a new credit for marine and hydrokinetic energy such as wave and tidal power.

Extends through 2014 the credits for solar, fuel cell, and microturbine property and for residential energy-efficient property, and adds new 30% credits for homeowners who install small wind turbines and geothermal heat pumps.

Directs the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to require detailed reporting from index traders and swap dealers in energy markets, publish monthly data separating index-fund positions from hedging positions, regulate certain trades on foreign exchanges, and hire at least 100 additional enforcement staff — a response to 2008 concerns that speculation was driving up gasoline prices.

Creates a Next Generation Energy and Efficiency Fund, capped at $40 billion, financed by half of the royalties from new offshore leases, to fund research on wind, solar, geothermal, hydrogen, smart grid, energy storage, and efficiency technologies.
Allows a tax credit for new plug-in electric drive vehicles, excludes bicycle-commuting reimbursements from taxable income, and extends credits for alternative fuel refueling stations.
Provides new clean renewable energy bonds — $2 billion of tax-credit bond financing — for public power providers, cooperatives, and governments to build renewable projects.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the financial risk of the coal-to-liquids standby loans — the government must pay projects whenever market prices fall below a set minimum — and fund the bill's tax credits and research authorizations. The federal treasury gives up a large share of new offshore royalties (half to a clean-energy research fund, 37.5% to coastal states). Coastal communities and ocean users bear the environmental risk of expanded offshore drilling and oil shale development.

drawbacks.text: The coal-to-liquids standby loans make the federal government a price-support backstop: if oil prices fall below a set minimum price, the Department of Energy must send the project payments based on its output, and projects can defer repayment whenever prices are below a cap price. Taxpayers bear the downside of low oil prices, with protection limited to an upfront payment estimated to cover the loan's cost.

The bill requires the Interior Department to offer for leasing essentially all inventoried Outer Continental Shelf areas outside the Gulf of Mexico — no drilling within 50 miles of a coast, or between 50 and 100 miles if a state objects — and strikes the appropriations-act language that had kept waters off California, the North Atlantic, Washington, and Oregon under moratoria, expanding drilling off currently protected coasts.
The bill delays until 2019 the special rules for worldwide allocation of interest in computing the foreign tax credit, a revenue-losing provision that benefits multinational corporations.
Oil shale leasing restrictions would be repealed, opening another federal fossil resource to development, though states could legislate to prohibit leasing on federal lands within their borders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was an explicit trade: more offshore drilling, oil shale, and federally backed coal-to-liquids loans on one side; long-term renewable tax credits, efficiency incentives, and new scrutiny of energy-market speculation on the other. The renewable and efficiency provisions were the strongest part for ordinary people — they would have extended wind, solar, and geothermal credits and let homeowners claim 30% credits for solar, wind, and geothermal heat pumps [S2][S3]. The coal-to-liquids standby loans were the weakest: they committed the federal government to pay projects whenever oil prices fell below a set floor, a taxpayer-backed price support for a carbon-intensive fuel, with the government's protection limited to an upfront payment meant to cover the loan's expected cost [S3]. Opening most of the Outer Continental Shelf to mandatory leasing offered possible supply gains but placed the environmental risk on coastal states and the wider public, with 37.5% of royalties going to affected states [S2][S3]. On balance, the bill delivered more certain value to energy industries than to households, and its most consumer-directed piece — the speculation-transparency title — was modest relative to the production and subsidy titles.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to five different House committees and then to subcommittees, none of which ever acted on it, so it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 1, 2008, near the end of the two-year congressional session, and referred the same day to five committees: Ways and Means, Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Science and Technology, and Agriculture.

Over the following two months it was passed down to three subcommittees (Energy and Air Quality, Energy and Mineral Resources, Energy and Environment, and General Farm Commodities), but no committee or subcommittee held a markup or reported the bill.
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died with it, never reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Groups that opposed expanded offshore drilling and taxpayer-backed coal-to-liquids loans were spared those policies, but so were the potential benefits lost: the renewable tax credits and the new energy-market speculation rules never happened either. The main beneficiaries of the bill's death were its fossil-energy targets' opponents and, more broadly, the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of offshore drilling and coal subsidies

for.name: Jim Matheson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 1, 2008, as a combined package of expanded domestic energy production, fossil and nuclear support, renewable tax credits, and energy-market speculation rules.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, a primary recipient of the referral, never took up the bill after it was referred on August 1, 2008.

against.name: Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, the first-listed recipient of the referral and holder of the entire tax title, never took up the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — a moderate wing of the party — and no Republican signed on, but the bill died in committee without a vote, so the parties' positions were never tested on the floor.

industries.note: The bill requires the Interior Department to inventory and then offer for lease nearly all federal offshore waters outside the Gulf of Mexico (with a 50-mile coastal buffer) and repeals oil shale leasing restrictions. Companies gain access to vast public resources; the public gains possible supply but bears the environmental risk, and states receive 37.5% of royalties.

Coal companies gain standby federal loans for up to six coal-to-liquids plants in which the government pays them when oil prices fall below a floor, plus an expanded $2.55 billion advanced coal investment credit. The public backs those price guarantees with tax dollars while the plants' carbon output is only capped at the emissions level of conventional petroleum refining.

Extended production and investment credits for wind, solar, geothermal, biomass, hydropower, and new marine energy, plus clean renewable energy bonds, channel federal support to the renewable industry. Because the credits also lower the cost of clean power and home installations, the industry's interest here runs alongside consumers'.

The bill reauthorizes the Nuclear Power 2010 Program (about $527 million over five years) with private-sector cost-sharing, creates an interagency group to promote nuclear exports and manufacturing, and funds workforce training. The industry gains federal cost-sharing and export promotion; the public benefit is framed as low-carbon power and jobs but depends on plants that take far longer than 2010 to build.

industries.industry: Energy futures traders and index funds
industries.note: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission gains authority over US persons trading on foreign exchanges, must publish monthly data on index-fund and speculative positions, and must hire at least 100 additional enforcement staff. This cuts into the anonymity and scale of speculative energy trading; the public benefit is greater price transparency in the markets that set gasoline prices.
